questions.question: At what point does partitioning become necessary?

options.text: When the dataset or the query throughput outgrows a single machine
As soon as more than one machine is available to the system
Whenever a secondary index has to be maintained
Only once replication has been exhausted as an option

questions.explanation: Partitioning, also called sharding, is for very large datasets or very high query throughput — the goal being to spread data and query load evenly across machines.

questions.question: Under what conditions is replication alone insufficient, and what is the second name for partitioning?

options.text: Very large datasets or very high query throughput; also called sharding
For very small datasets or low throughput; the alternative is called mirroring
For read-heavy workloads; the alternative is called caching
For write-heavy workloads; the alternative is called batching

questions.explanation: Replication means having multiple copies of the same data on different nodes; partitioning means breaking it up so each node holds a subset.

questions.question: The word 'partition' names two unrelated things. Which two?

options.text: Deliberately splitting a database, versus a network fault between nodes
Disk partitions on one machine, versus database partitions across machines
Horizontal partitioning of rows, versus vertical partitioning of columns
Logical partition boundaries, versus the physical files that hold them

questions.explanation: Netsplits are a fault; sharding is a design choice. The word is badly overloaded.

questions.question: Different systems use different words for a partition. Which pairings are right? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: shard in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and SolrCloud
region in HBase, and tablet in Bigtable
vnode in Cassandra and Riak, and vBucket in Couchbase
chunk in Kafka and segment in Voldemort

questions.explanation: Shard, region, tablet, vnode and vBucket are product-specific names for a partition. Kafka commonly calls its unit a partition, so the chunk/segment pairing is incorrect.

questions.question: How many logical partitions normally own a record?

options.text: Exactly one, though replicas may copy it
Each record belongs to several partitions for redundancy; the caveat is that reads must query all of them
Each record belongs to exactly one node; the caveat is that nodes may fail
Records are assigned randomly; the caveat is that reads are slow

questions.explanation: Partitioning assigns each record to one logical partition; replication may then place copies of that partition on several nodes. Treating a partition as a small database is only a metaphor because operations can still span partitions.

questions.question: Why partition at all, and what two distinct resources get spread?

options.text: For scalability, across many disks and many processors in a shared-nothing cluster
For availability, so that the failure of any one node does not lose data
For latency, so that each partition sits geographically close to its users
For durability, so that an acknowledged write survives a machine crash

questions.explanation: Two resources, not one: storage and compute. Those other three are replication's benefits.

questions.question: How does partitioning affect query scalability?

options.text: Local queries scale; cross-partition coordination is harder
Every query scales linearly with the node count, with no hedge attached
Only single-partition queries can be parallelized, never complex ones
Complex queries scale better than simple ones, since they touch more nodes

questions.explanation: Independent single-partition requests scale naturally because each node serves its own subset. Large analytical queries can parallelize scans and stages, but coordinating joins, aggregation, and result exchange is substantially harder.

questions.question: Which systems pioneered partitioned databases?

options.text: Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL in the 1980s
In the 1990s by Oracle and DB2; rediscovered by cloud vendors
In the 2000s by Google; rediscovered by relational databases
In the 1970s by IBM IMS; rediscovered by document databases

questions.explanation: Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL pioneered partitioned databases in the 1980s. NoSQL databases and Hadoop data warehouses later rediscovered the same core idea of dividing data and work across machines.

questions.question: Some partitioned systems target transactional workloads and others analytics. What does that difference affect, and what does it not?

options.text: It changes how the system is tuned, not the fundamentals of partitioning
It changes the partitioning algorithm itself, which differs entirely between the two
It changes nothing at all, since partitioning is invisible to the workload
It changes the replication scheme, though the tuning stays the same

questions.explanation: Transactional systems optimize many small, low-latency requests, while analytical systems optimize large scans and parallel stages. Both still face the same core placement, skew and rebalancing problems.

questions.question: A colleague reads that each record belongs to exactly one partition and concludes it lives on exactly one machine. Correct them.

options.text: A record belongs to one partition but may be stored on several nodes
They are correct: one partition always means exactly one machine
Each record is stored on every machine in the cluster at once
Records are moved between machines on every read to balance load

questions.explanation: Partition membership is logical; node placement is physical, and replication decouples the two.

questions.question: When partitioning is combined with leader–follower replication, how are leaders and followers placed?

options.text: Each node leads some partitions and follows others
One node is leader for all partitions and the rest are followers
Each partition has its own dedicated node with no replication
All nodes are leaders for all partitions

questions.explanation: A balanced replicated cluster spreads leadership rather than assigning one global leader. Each node leads some partitions and stores follower copies of others, distributing writes and failover capacity.

questions.question: How are partitioning and replication related?

options.text: They are mostly independent design choices
Partitioning fully determines the replication scheme, so both must be chosen together
Replication must be disabled when partitioning is used
The two are entirely independent with no qualification

questions.explanation: Partitioning decides which logical subset owns a record; replication decides how many copies of that subset exist and how they stay consistent. They can usually be chosen separately, although placement and failover policies must coordinate both.

questions.question: State the arithmetic ideal for fair partitioning.

options.text: Ten nodes should handle ten times the data and ten times the throughput
Ten nodes should handle roughly twice the data of a single node
Ten nodes should handle ten times the data but the same throughput
Throughput scales with nodes while total data volume does not

questions.explanation: Ignoring replication overhead, ideal horizontal scaling is linear: ten comparable nodes hold about ten times the data and serve about ten times the throughput of one.

questions.question: What are skew and a hot spot in a partitioned system?

options.text: Skew is uneven load; a hot spot is an overloaded partition
Skew means clock drift between nodes; a hot spot is an overheated machine
Skew means variance in network latency; a hot spot is a cache miss storm
Skew means having too many partitions; a hot spot means having too few

questions.explanation: Skew means data or requests are distributed unevenly, and the disproportionately busy partition is a hot spot. In the extreme, one partition serves all traffic while nine of ten nodes sit idle, defeating horizontal scaling.

questions.question: Random assignment would avoid hot spots. What does it get right, and what is the big disadvantage?

options.text: Even distribution, but every read must query all nodes in parallel
It distributes the data unevenly but makes every read very fast
It is optimal in every respect, which is why real systems use it
It blocks range queries entirely while allowing fast point lookups

questions.explanation: Random placement balances data, but it provides no deterministic route from a key to its node. Every lookup would become a scatter/gather request, trading balanced writes for expensive reads.

questions.question: What information enables direct routing with key-range partitioning?

options.text: Range boundaries and the partition-to-node map
Assign keys by hash; you need only the hash function to route
Assign keys randomly; routing requires a lookup service
Assign keys round-robin; routing requires a counter

questions.explanation: Key-range partitioning assigns each partition a continuous interval of keys. A client can route directly only if it knows both the interval boundaries and which node currently owns each interval.

questions.question: In a print encyclopedia, volume 1 covers A and B while volume 12 covers T through Z. What design conclusion follows?

options.text: Ranges need not be evenly spaced, because the data isn't evenly distributed
Both volumes cover exactly two letters, which proves even spacing works
Volume 1 covers only A while volume 12 covers only Z
The volumes are hash-partitioned, so their contents are arbitrary

questions.explanation: Alphabetic data is not evenly distributed, so equal-sized letter ranges would create unequal volumes. Key-range boundaries should adapt to the actual data distribution rather than visual symmetry.

questions.question: Who picks partition boundaries, and which systems use key-range partitioning? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Boundaries might be chosen manually by an administrator, or the database can choose them automatically
Bigtable and its open source equivalent HBase
RethinkDB, and MongoDB before version 2.4
Cassandra and Riak, which use a compound primary key

questions.explanation: Cassandra and Riak are hash-partitioned. MongoDB's version qualifier matters — it changed after 2.4.

questions.question: What does keeping keys sorted within each partition buy?

options.text: Range scans, using the key as a concatenated index over related records
Point lookups become constant time rather than logarithmic
Cross-partition joins become possible without extra coordination
Writes become sequential, removing the need for compaction

questions.explanation: Because keys remain ordered within a partition, the storage engine can scan a contiguous interval efficiently. Compound keys can use this ordering as an index over related records such as one user's timestamped events.

questions.question: If sensor measurements are key-range partitioned by an increasing timestamp, what hot-spot failure occurs?

options.text: A timestamp key sends all of today's writes to one partition
Reads scatter across all partitions, making range queries slow
Partitions grow without bound and cannot be split
Timestamps cannot be used as keys at all

questions.explanation: All current timestamps fall at the high end of the key space, so today's writes concentrate on the one partition owning that range. Older partitions receive little or no write traffic.

questions.question: How can timestamp-keyed sensor writes avoid one hot partition?

options.text: Prefix each timestamp with the sensor ID
Switch entirely to hash partitioning, which costs nothing in practice
Add more partitions per day, at the cost of extra disk consumption
Buffer the writes in memory, at the cost of weakened durability

questions.explanation: A sensor-ID prefix sends different sensors' current writes to different key ranges. The trade-off is that a time-range query across all sensors must query and combine many sensor-specific ranges.

questions.question: A partitioning hash function maps a string key to a 32-bit value. What is its output range and key property?

options.text: A number from 0 to 2 to the 32nd minus 1, evenly spread even for similar inputs
It returns a number between 0 and 2 to the 16th; similar inputs produce similar hashes
It returns a number between 1 and 100; distribution depends on input
It returns a cryptographic digest of 256 bits

questions.explanation: A 32-bit hash produces values from 0 through 2^32 - 1. Good avalanche behavior spreads even similar input keys throughout that range instead of preserving a hot source-key neighborhood.

questions.question: What properties should a database partitioning hash have?

options.text: Stable, repeatable output with a uniform distribution
It must be cryptographically strong, so SHA-256 is effectively required
Any built-in hash will do, including Java's Object.hashCode() method
It must be reversible, so that the original key can be recovered

questions.explanation: A partition hash needs repeatable, well-distributed output rather than cryptographic strength. Language runtimes may randomize built-in hashes between processes, so systems use stable algorithms such as MD5 or FNV instead.

questions.question: How does hash partitioning assign keys to partitions?

options.text: Map each key into a partition's hash-value range
Assign each partition a range of keys; boundaries are always evenly spaced
Assign each key a random partition; boundaries do not exist
Assign each partition a fixed number of keys; boundaries are recomputed on every write

questions.explanation: Hashing converts arbitrary keys into a bounded numeric space, and each partition owns a range in that space. The range boundaries may be evenly spaced or chosen pseudorandomly.

questions.question: What is consistent hashing as originally defined?

options.text: Karger et al.'s scheme for spreading load across internet-wide caches
A database rebalancing algorithm defined by Amazon for the Dynamo paper
A hash function whose output stays stable across separate processes
A method for maintaining key order within a single partition

questions.explanation: Karger-style consistent hashing assigns cache objects around a hash ring so membership changes move relatively few objects. It was designed for decentralized internet caches, not as a general name for database hash partitioning.

questions.question: Where is Karger's consistent hashing most suitable?

options.text: Decentralized internet caches and CDNs
It endorses consistent hashing as the standard database rebalancing method
It denies that consistent hashing exists
It recommends using the term consistent hashing for all hash-based schemes

questions.explanation: Karger's consistent hashing was designed for decentralized caches and CDNs. Its random boundaries are awkward for database rebalancing, and database products often use the same name for materially different placement schemes.

questions.question: What important capability does hash partitioning sacrifice?

options.text: Ordered, efficient primary-key range queries
The ability to do point lookups; all four systems lose them
The ability to rebalance; only MongoDB is affected
Nothing of value is lost, because hash partitioning is strictly better

questions.explanation: Hashing spreads adjacent source keys across unrelated hash values, so a range query must scatter rather than scan one ordered interval. MongoDB hash sharding does this; Riak, Couchbase and Voldemort omit primary-key range queries.

questions.question: How does Cassandra partition and order a compound primary key?

options.text: Hash the first component; sort by the rest
Hash the entire compound key and discard component ordering
Keep the first component ordered and use the rest only for routing
Hash the final component and use earlier components as clustering keys

questions.explanation: The first component keeps one entity's related rows together, while the remaining columns provide an ordered index inside that partition. It cannot efficiently range-scan across different first-component values.

questions.question: Which data shape suits Cassandra's compound-key scheme?

options.text: One-to-many records grouped by their parent
Many-to-many relationships, which are handled with a graph data model
Analytics queries that aggregate across every user simultaneously
Full-text search over the bodies of the posted updates themselves

questions.explanation: The first key component identifies the 'one' side, such as a user, keeping its related rows together. Remaining components, such as timestamps, then provide useful ordering within that partition.

questions.question: Hashing reduces hot spots but can't avoid them entirely. What is the extreme case, and why is hashing powerless?

options.text: All reads and writes for one key still land on a single partition
The extreme case is too many distinct keys; hashing collides them
The extreme case is an empty database; hashing has nothing to distribute
Hashing does avoid all hot spots

questions.explanation: A deterministic hash must send every occurrence of the same key to the same partition. If one key receives nearly all traffic, no uniform distribution across different keys can split that single-key load.

questions.question: How can an application spread writes to a known-hot key?

options.text: Append a random suffix and fan reads out
Add a timestamp suffix, producing unbounded fan-out with no read cost
Replicate the key to all nodes, producing n copies with no read cost
Move the key to a dedicated node, producing a fan-out of 1

questions.explanation: Adding two random decimal digits turns one logical key into 100 physical keys, spreading writes across partitions. Reads must query and combine all 100 suffixes, so write relief is purchased with read fan-out.

questions.question: Besides querying every suffix, which bookkeeping costs does random-suffix splitting of a hot key introduce? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It requires additional bookkeeping, so it only makes sense to apply it to the small number of hot keys — for the vast majority of keys with low write throughput this would be unnecessary overhead
You need some way of keeping track of which keys are being split
It requires the hash function to be cryptographically strong, or the split is uneven
It requires replication to be disabled while the split key is in use

questions.explanation: Overhead plus new state to maintain, which is why splitting can't be applied blanket-wide.

questions.question: Who normally handles a known hot key today?

options.text: The application must usually reduce the skew
Databases compensate for this automatically today, so applications need not care
It is the operations team's responsibility rather than the application's
Skew of this kind cannot be reduced by the application or the database

questions.explanation: Most databases can rebalance partitions but cannot recognize the application meaning of one exceptionally hot key. The application therefore usually shards or redesigns that key, though future systems may automate more of this.

questions.question: What are the two main ways to partition a secondary index?

options.text: Locally by document or globally by indexed term
A secondary index uniquely identifies a record; the approaches are local and remote
A secondary index is a copy of the primary index; the approaches are eager and lazy
A secondary index is a cache; the approaches are write-through and write-back

questions.explanation: A secondary index locates records by non-primary values such as color or make. It can be stored locally with each document partition or globally partitioned by the indexed term.

questions.question: How does secondary-index support vary across systems? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Secondary indexes are the bread and butter of relational databases, and they are common in document databases too
Many key-value stores such as HBase and Voldemort have avoided secondary indexes because of their added implementation complexity
Redis and Memcached have both added secondary index support in recent releases
Secondary indexes are the raison d'être of search servers such as Solr and Elasticsearch

questions.explanation: Relational and document databases commonly support secondary indexes, while search servers are built around them. Some key-value stores avoid their coordination cost; Redis and Memcached do not provide general secondary indexes.

questions.question: On a used-car site partitioned by document ID, with IDs 0-499 in partition 0 and 500-999 in partition 1, which partition holds document ID 742?

options.text: Partition 1, since IDs 500 to 999 live there
Partition 0, since 742 modulo 500 is 242
Both partitions, since the index is global
Neither partition, because the ID 742 falls outside the configured range

questions.explanation: Document ID 742 falls inside the explicitly stated 500–999 range, so partition 1 owns it. The calculation depends only on the primary-key boundary; secondary fields such as color or make do not change document placement.

questions.question: If your database offers only a key-value model, which hazards should you watch for? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Race conditions
Intermittent write failures, where some changes were saved but others weren't
Hash collisions between two different secondary index keys
Fragmentation of the index file as documents are updated

questions.explanation: An application-maintained index updates both the source record and a value-to-ID mapping. Concurrent writers or a partial failure between those writes can make them disagree, so atomic multi-object updates or careful repair are needed.

questions.question: What must a write update with document-partitioned indexing?

options.text: Its owning data partition and that partition's indexes
Each write must update the index on every partition; it is called a global index
Each write updates a central index server; it is called a remote index
Writes do not touch the index at all; it is rebuilt nightly

questions.explanation: Each partition indexes only its own documents, so a write updates the record and local index on one partition. That cheap write path is the main benefit; reads may need scatter/gather.

questions.question: How is a document-partitioned secondary index queried?

options.text: Scatter to every partition and gather the results
Reads must be serialized across partitions, which is slow but has bounded latency
Reads can only target one partition, missing results
Reads require a distributed transaction

questions.explanation: A local secondary index contains matches only from its own data partition. The coordinator must query every partition and wait for the slowest relevant response, so scatter/gather amplifies tail latency.

questions.question: Which systems use document-partitioned secondary indexes, and what do most vendors recommend? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud and VoltDB all use them
Most database vendors recommend that you structure your partitioning scheme so that secondary index queries can be served from a single partition
That recommendation is not always possible, especially when you're using multiple secondary indexes in a single query — such as filtering cars by color and by make at the same time
Vendors recommend always using term-partitioned indexes instead, since reads dominate

questions.explanation: Document-partitioned indexes keep writes local and are therefore common, but a query may need every partition. Choosing a partition key that serves common index queries locally avoids scatter/gather when the access pattern permits it.

questions.question: Why must a global index itself be partitioned?

options.text: Because a single global index on one node would become the bottleneck
Because a secondary index is always larger than the data it indexes
Because no single node is capable of holding an entire index at all
It need not be partitioned at all; one dedicated index node suffices

questions.explanation: The freedom to partition the index differently from the primary key is what makes term partitioning useful.

questions.question: In a term-partitioned index on colour, where do the partition boundaries fall?

options.text: Colors a to r in partition 0, s to z in partition 1
Colors a to m in partition 0 and n to z in partition 1; makes a to l and m to z
The index is not partitioned, living entirely on one node
The index is partitioned by document ID, like the primary index

questions.explanation: The index is partitioned differently from the primary key index, which is exactly what makes it global.

questions.question: What determines the partition in a term-partitioned index?

options.text: The indexed term, such as color:red
Because the index terminates at a partition boundary; the word comes from mathematics
Because terms are contract clauses; the word comes from legal indexing
Because the partition is determined by the document, not the term

questions.explanation: The indexed value chooses the partition, so all entries for color:red can reside together. The word 'term' comes from full-text search, where each indexed word is a search term.

questions.question: What trade-off comes from hashing secondary-index terms?

options.text: More even load, but no ordered range scans
By the term gives even load, while hashing the term enables range scans
Both choices support range scans, and neither affects load distribution
Hashing changes placement but preserves the original term order

questions.explanation: The same order-versus-uniformity trade-off as for primary keys, now applied to the index.

questions.question: How does a term-partitioned index shift query cost?

options.text: Reads get cheaper; writes get costlier
Reads become slower while writes become faster and simpler
Both reads and writes become faster than with a local index
Both reads and writes become slower than with a local index

questions.explanation: A term points directly to one global index partition, avoiding read scatter/gather. Updating a document may affect several term partitions, moving coordination and latency onto the write path.

questions.question: What would an always-up-to-date term-partitioned index require?

options.text: A distributed transaction across every affected partition
Only a local transaction on the partition being written to
A nightly batch job that rebuilds the whole index from scratch
Independent local transactions on the data and index partitions

questions.explanation: Keeping a global term index immediately current may require one atomic transaction across the data partition and every affected index partition. Systems commonly avoid that coordination by updating the index asynchronously.

questions.question: How are global secondary indexes usually updated?

options.text: Asynchronously, creating a temporary stale-index window
Synchronously within a distributed transaction; DynamoDB guarantees immediate consistency
Once per day in a batch job; DynamoDB rebuilds nightly
On read, lazily; DynamoDB has no global indexes

questions.explanation: Synchronous maintenance may require a distributed transaction across several index partitions. Asynchronous propagation avoids that write-path coordination but temporarily leaves the index stale; DynamoDB usually propagates quickly without a hard fault-time bound.

questions.question: What changes over time that necessitates rebalancing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The query throughput increases, so you want to add more CPUs to handle the load
The dataset size increases, so you want to add more disks and RAM to store it
A machine fails, and other machines need to take over the failed machine's responsibilities
The document schema changes, which forces the whole index to be rebuilt

questions.explanation: The process of moving load from one node in the cluster to another is called rebalancing.

questions.question: What are the minimum requirements rebalancing is expected to meet? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: After rebalancing, the load — data storage, read and write requests — should be shared fairly between the nodes in the cluster
While rebalancing is happening, the database should continue accepting reads and writes
No more data than necessary should be moved between nodes, to make rebalancing fast and to minimize the network and disk I/O load
Rebalancing should always complete within a fixed, configurable time bound

questions.explanation: Good rebalancing restores fair storage and request load, keeps reads and writes available during movement, and transfers only necessary data. A universal fixed completion time is unrealistic under variable data and network load.

questions.question: A key hashes to 123456. Under hash mod N, which node does it land on with 10, 11, 12 and 13 nodes?

options.text: Nodes 6, 3, 0 and 8 — the mod-10 result is the last digit
On node 6 in all four cases, since the hash is fixed
On node 0, 1, 2 and 3 respectively, in sequence
The key cannot be placed without a lookup table

questions.explanation: Changing N reshuffles almost everything, which is exactly what rebalancing must avoid.

questions.question: How does fixed partitioning rebalance when a node joins?

options.text: Move whole pre-created partitions to the new node
The number of partitions increases to 1,100 and all data is rehashed
The new node receives 100 partitions and the others keep theirs
All 1,000 partitions are redistributed from scratch

questions.explanation: Fixed partitioning creates many more partitions than nodes and changes only their node assignments during rebalancing. With 1,000 partitions spread across 11 nodes, the newcomer receives roughly 91.

questions.question: In the fixed-partition scheme, what changes during rebalancing and what does not?

options.text: Only whole partitions move; the key-to-partition mapping never changes
Keys are reassigned to different partitions, and partition count grows
The number of partitions changes but key assignment stays fixed
All three change simultaneously

questions.explanation: The hash or range rule continues mapping each key to the same fixed logical partition. Rebalancing changes only which physical node owns that whole partition, limiting remapping and data movement.

questions.question: Your cluster has some much more powerful machines. What does the fixed-partition scheme let you do?

options.text: Give more partitions to more powerful nodes
Nothing can be done, because every node must hold an equal partition count
Give the powerful nodes larger partitions
Disable rebalancing on the weaker nodes

questions.explanation: Because partitions are independent placement units, a stronger machine can own more of them than a weaker machine. Partition counts thereby approximate each node's storage and throughput capacity.

questions.question: What scaling ceiling follows from a fixed partition count?

options.text: The cluster cannot exceed its partition count
HBase and RethinkDB, with no ceiling on node count
Cassandra and Riak, with a ceiling of 256 nodes
MongoDB and Bigtable, with no management overhead

questions.explanation: Each node needs at least one partition, so the fixed count caps the node count unless splitting is added. Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase and Voldemort use this model. Too few partitions become large and costly to move; too many add overhead.

questions.question: How do HBase and RethinkDB adapt uneven key ranges?

options.text: Split large ranges and merge small adjacent ranges
They use hash partitioning instead, avoiding the problem
They require the administrator to preconfigure exact boundaries
They never split partitions, relying on large nodes

questions.explanation: Fixed key boundaries can leave one range holding most of the data. Dynamic range partitioning behaves like a B-tree: oversized ranges split, while small neighboring ranges merge.

questions.question: What happens after a dynamic key-range partition splits?

options.text: One half may move to another node
Both halves stay on the original node; the advantage is simplicity
Both halves move to new nodes; the advantage is even distribution
The halves are merged back; the advantage is stability

questions.explanation: The two halves remain separate logical partitions, and the system may move one half to balance load. Each partition has one owner while a node may own many; the partition count grows with data volume.

questions.question: How can dynamic range partitioning avoid a cold-start hot spot?

options.text: Pre-split the expected key ranges
An empty database starts with many partitions; the mitigation is merging
Dynamic partitioning is already optimal for an empty database, so no mitigation is needed
The caveat is that partitions never split; the mitigation is manual splitting

questions.explanation: An empty database may begin with one partition, concentrating all early writes on one node. Pre-splitting distributes those writes immediately, but requires advance knowledge of the likely key distribution.

questions.question: True or false: dynamic partitioning applies only to key range–partitioned data.

options.text: False — it works with hash partitioning too, as MongoDB shows
True — hash partitioning always uses a fixed number of partitions
True — only HBase and RethinkDB support it, and both are key-range
False — it applies only to hash-partitioned data

questions.explanation: Dynamic partitioning means partitions can split as they grow; it does not require source-key ranges. MongoDB can split ranges of hash values just as another system splits ranges of original keys.

questions.question: Three partitioning schemes differ in what is proportional to what. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: With dynamic partitioning, the number of partitions is proportional to dataset size
With a fixed number of partitions, the size of each partition is proportional to dataset size
In both of those cases, the number of partitions grows in step with the number of nodes
With a fixed number of partitions per node, partition count is proportional to node count

questions.explanation: Dynamic partitioning keeps partition size within bounds, so partition count grows with data. A fixed-count design instead lets each partition grow with the dataset. Cassandra/Ketama-style designs keep partitions per node roughly fixed, so total partition count grows with node count.

questions.question: How does partitioning proportional to nodes add a new node?

options.text: Split selected partitions and give it one half of each
The new node takes whole partitions from existing nodes, with no splitting
All partitions are recomputed from scratch, doubling the count
The new node creates 256 empty partitions and waits for writes

questions.explanation: The new node chooses a fixed number of existing partitions, splits them, and takes one half of each. Cassandra historically used about 256 partitions per node so many random shares average toward fair load.

questions.question: Why does picking partition boundaries randomly require hash-based partitioning?

options.text: Because boundaries can be sampled from the hash function's numeric range
Because hashing is what makes the keys sortable in the first place
Because raw keys cannot be compared to one another at all
It does not require hashing; raw keys work equally well for sampling

questions.explanation: A hash function maps arbitrary keys into a known numeric space, so a joining node can select boundary positions without knowing the original key distribution. Raw ordered keys generally do not offer that uniform numeric space.

questions.question: What is the middle ground between automatic and manual rebalancing?

options.text: The system proposes a plan; an administrator approves it
Only fully automatic and fully manual exist; there is no middle
The middle position is automatic detection with manual data movement
All systems are fully automatic

questions.explanation: Fully automatic systems both decide and move partitions; fully manual systems leave both tasks to an operator. A common compromise lets software compute a rebalancing plan but requires human approval before movement.

questions.question: Why is fully automated rebalancing risky?

options.text: Because rebalancing moves a lot of data and can overload the network
Because a partition transfer can corrupt data while it is in flight
Because it requires the database to be taken offline while it runs
It carries no real risk, so full automation is always the better choice

questions.explanation: Moving partitions consumes network bandwidth, disk I/O and CPU on both source and destination nodes. Fully automatic movement at the wrong moment can worsen the overload that triggered it.

questions.question: How can automatic rebalancing amplify an overloaded-node failure?

options.text: It adds load after mistaking slowness for failure
A node fails, rebalancing succeeds, and the cluster recovers automatically
A network partition causes two clusters to form and diverge
A disk fills up and rebalancing frees space

questions.explanation: Automatic rebalancing plus automatic failure detection is a positive feedback loop under load.

questions.question: What is finding the correct current node for a request called?

options.text: Service discovery
Load balancing across the available nodes
Distributed consensus between the nodes
Rebalancing of partitions across nodes

questions.explanation: Partition ownership changes during rebalancing, so a client needs a current IP address and port for the node serving its key. That changing endpoint lookup is the general service-discovery problem.

questions.question: Which routing strategies can send a request to its partition?

options.text: Node forwarding, a routing tier, or direct client routing
DNS, load balancing and gossip; the shared problem is latency
Client-side, server-side and proxy routing; the shared problem is security
Hash, range and random routing; the shared problem is skew

questions.explanation: Routing logic may live in a database node, an external partition-aware tier, or the client. Every design still needs a sufficiently current and consistent partition-to-node map after rebalancing.

questions.question: How does a coordination service solve request routing?

options.text: A separate coordination service such as ZooKeeper holds the mapping
The nodes gossip the mapping among themselves, with no central service
The client polls every node in the cluster on every single request
A dedicated DNS server holds the authoritative partition mapping

questions.explanation: All participants must agree, so all participants must read the same authoritative place.

questions.question: Which systems use the ZooKeeper-style approach? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: LinkedIn's Espresso, which uses Helix for cluster management — and Helix in turn relies on ZooKeeper
HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka, which also use ZooKeeper to track partition assignment
MongoDB, which has a similar architecture but relies on its own config server implementation and mongos daemons as the routing tier
Cassandra and Riak, which both rely on gossip between nodes

questions.explanation: Espresso/Helix, HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka use ZooKeeper-style coordination for partition assignments; MongoDB uses analogous config servers and mongos routers. Cassandra and Riak instead gossip state among database nodes.

questions.question: What routing approach do Cassandra and Riak use?

options.text: Nodes gossip mappings and forward requests
They use a dedicated routing tier, which reduces node complexity but adds a dependency
They require partition-aware clients, which removes all server complexity
They use DNS for routing, which is simple but slow to update

questions.explanation: Cassandra and Riak spread cluster-state changes by gossip, and any node can forward a request to the owner. This removes an external coordinator but moves membership and routing complexity into every node.

questions.question: How does Couchbase handle routing and rebalancing?

options.text: Couchbase doesn't rebalance automatically, and uses a routing tier called moxi
Couchbase relies on ZooKeeper and rebalances partitions automatically
Couchbase uses gossip and requires every client to be partition-aware
Couchbase has no routing layer, so clients address nodes directly

questions.explanation: A design consequence of the earlier rebalancing choice — no automatic rebalancing means less routing churn to disseminate.

questions.question: How can clients discover router or seed-node addresses?

options.text: Use DNS or a stable seed-node list
Clients must be configured with a static list of every node's IP address
Clients must query ZooKeeper directly to obtain the IP addresses
Clients must broadcast on the local network to discover the nodes

questions.explanation: Router and seed-node addresses change far less often than individual partition assignments. DNS or a configured seed list can therefore bootstrap contact, after which the system supplies current routing metadata.

questions.question: Which query shapes are supported by simple partitioning alone, and how far do most NoSQL distributed datastores go?

options.text: Single-key reads and writes, plus scatter/gather for local secondary indexes
Full SQL with joins and aggregation, which every NoSQL store supports
Only single-key reads and writes, with no scatter/gather capability
Only analytics queries that scan the whole of the dataset

questions.explanation: Simple distributed stores usually handle primary-key operations and sometimes scatter/gather secondary-index queries. Joins, grouping and complex cross-partition plans require a parallel query engine such as those in MPP databases.

questions.question: What does an MPP query optimizer do?

options.text: Splits a query into parallel stages and data partitions
Multi-partition processing; the optimizer routes each query to one node
Message passing protocol; the optimizer serializes execution
Modular parallel partitioning; the optimizer only handles joins

questions.explanation: MPP means massively parallel processing. Its optimizer turns scans, joins and aggregation into dependent execution stages, partitions each stage's work across nodes, and combines their results.

questions.question: Which queries particularly benefit from parallel execution across partitions?

options.text: Queries that scan large parts of the dataset
Single-key point lookups by primary key
Reads that hit one local secondary index
Writes that update a single small record

questions.explanation: A scan over much of the dataset can divide independent ranges among many nodes and combine their partial results. A single-key lookup already targets one small location, so cross-node parallelism adds overhead rather than useful work.

questions.question: When is database partitioning necessary?

options.text: When one machine cannot hold or serve the workload
Partitioning is necessary whenever you have more than one machine; the goal is fault tolerance
Partitioning is necessary for read scaling; the goal is low latency
Partitioning is necessary when replication fails; the goal is durability

questions.explanation: Partitioning is justified when one machine cannot store the data or serve the workload. Its benefit depends on both a suitable key-to-partition rule and rebalancing as data, traffic, or cluster membership changes.

questions.question: Describe key range partitioning and its trade-off.

options.text: Sorted keys, each partition owning a range — good for range queries, risky for hot spots
Keys are hashed and a partition owns a range of hashes; range queries are inefficient
Keys are assigned randomly; there is no hot spot risk
Keys are sorted but partitions are fixed in number and never split

questions.explanation: Each partition owns a contiguous, sorted key range, enabling efficient scans over nearby keys. Uneven or increasing keys can create hot spots, so systems often adjust boundaries by splitting and merging ranges.

questions.question: What is the central trade-off of hash partitioning?

options.text: Smoother load at the cost of ordered range queries
It preserves the ordering of keys and guarantees an even distribution
It destroys ordering and guarantees even distribution, with no hedging
It preserves ordering but may distribute the load quite unevenly

questions.explanation: A good hash smooths ordinary key distributions but cannot eliminate application-level hot keys, so evenness is not guaranteed. The cost is that adjacent source keys become unrelated hash values and cannot be scanned together efficiently.

questions.question: Which hybrid of the two partitioning schemes is possible?

options.text: A compound key: one part selects the partition, another gives the sort order
Combining local and global secondary indexes in one database
Combining a fixed partition count with dynamic partition splitting
Combining replication with partitioning in the same cluster

questions.explanation: A compound key can hash its first component to spread parent entities across partitions, then sort by remaining components inside each partition. This supports local range scans without preserving global key order.

questions.question: Restate both secondary-index partitioning methods with their costs. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Document-partitioned indexes (local indexes), where the secondary indexes are stored in the same partition as the primary key and value
With local indexes only a single partition needs to be updated on write, but a read of the secondary index requires a scatter/gather across all partitions

Term-partitioned indexes (global indexes), where the secondary indexes are partitioned separately using the indexed values, so an entry in the global index may include records from all partitions of the primary key
With global indexes a write touches only one index partition, while a read must scatter/gather across all of them

questions.explanation: That describes local indexes, not global ones. With global (term-partitioned) indexes a write must update several index partitions, but a read can be served from a single one. Local: cheap writes, expensive reads. Global: expensive writes, cheap reads.

questions.question: Which of these claims about partitioning hold? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Consistent hashing as originally defined works poorly for databases, so hash partitioning is the better term
In fixed-partition rebalancing the assignment of keys to partitions does not change; only the assignment of partitions to nodes does
A term-partitioned index can be partitioned differently from the primary key index
Hashing a key eliminates hot spots entirely, even for a single hot key

questions.explanation: Hashing can help reduce hot spots, but it can't avoid them entirely — the hash of two identical IDs is still the same.

questions.question: How should request routing be thought about?

options.text: As a spectrum, from partition-aware load balancing to parallel query engines
As a binary choice between client-side and server-side request routing
As a single recommended architecture built around ZooKeeper
As an unsolved problem that every deployment must tackle afresh

questions.explanation: Routing ranges from choosing one node for a simple key lookup, through scatter/gather across several partitions, to an MPP engine coordinating a multi-stage parallel plan. These are degrees of partition awareness, not a binary choice.

questions.question: Which property makes partitioning work, and which problem does it create?

options.text: Partitions operate independently, but cross-partition writes are hard to reason about
Partitions are tightly coupled, which is what makes cross-partition writes easy
Partitions share one global lock, which is what limits scalability
Partitions are replicated, which is what makes cross-partition writes slow

questions.explanation: Independence buys scale and costs cross-partition atomicity — which is exactly what transactions are for.
